SCHÜRER (1890)
Ethnarch from Herod's death in 4 BC until Augustus deposed him and banished him to Vienne in Gaul in AD 6.
Yes, the story echoes his journey to Rome
H. A. W. Meyer (English 1880); F. W. Farrar (1880); C. J. Ellicott's commentary (about 1880); A. B. Bruce (1897), who says the idea has been "very generally accepted" since Clericus and Wolf

A nobleman goes "into a far country to receive for himself a kingdom" and his citizens send after him, "We will not have this man to reign over us". They compare Archelaus's journey to Augustus and the embassy of fifty sent against him (Antiquities 17.11.1); Farrar notes that Herod and Archelaus had both gone from Jericho to Rome to receive a kingdom, and Jesus told the parable near Jericho (Luke 19:1, 11). Luke 19:1 Luke 19:11–14 [23][20][4][1]
Jesus would not have pictured himself by Archelaus
Schanz, as reported by A. B. Bruce (1897), who disagrees
Bruce reports Schanz's objection that Jesus would not choose so bad a man to stand for himself, and answers that Jesus also used an unjust judge and an unjust steward in parables. Luke 19:12 [1]

WHAT SCRIPTURE DOES NOT SAY
Scripture names Archelaus once (Matthew 2:22) and records nothing he did.
Scripture does not call him king or ethnarch; it says he "did reign".
Scripture does not record his removal by Augustus.
Luke's parable of the nobleman (Luke 19:12) names no ruler.
IDENTIFICATIONS THIS PAGE RELIES ON
Matthew names him once, as son of Herod: "Archelaus did reign in Judaea in the room of his father Herod". Matthew 2:22

Scholars' viewSchürer (1890) assigns him the coins inscribed, in Greek, "of Herod the ethnarch", since no other Herodian bore that title, and notes that the Roman historian Dio Cassius calls him Herod.[18]
